items.title: Bobby Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: And there was a few fellows like him — Marty Grosz, Frank Chace, Frank Orchard, Tut Soper, there was Little Brother Montgomery, there was Bob Skiver

ctx.x: Well it’s changed quite a bit. In the old days, I guess in New Orleans in the 1920s and even before that, they called it Dixieland jazz and they had mostly blacks playing that

type of music. And now, in the 90s now they have a whole different type of combinations of Dixieland bands. The name “Dixieland” is really a bad term because it puts a label on the type of music that actually was played. Actually it’s called “classic jazz” or “traditional jazz,” that’s what I like to call it. And back in the 20s when they had Johnny Dodds and Louis Armstrong and oh — Jimmy Noone, Mancy Carr, Lillie Delk Christian, Earl Hines, all these different stars in jazz in the 20s, were black artists. And…

It’s great to see young guys doing what I guess, what would we call — sometimes we don’t want to put a label on everything — but what we’ll hear tonight at this festival. Do you have a name for the style?
